content: 1. All pregnant and breastfeeding women living with HIV should initiate a regimen of triple antiretroviral (ARV) drugs, also known as antiretroviral therapy (ART). This treatment should be maintained for at least the duration of the period when there is a risk of mother-to-child transmission of HIV. Women who meet the criteria for lifelong treatment should continue ART indefinitely, as strongly recommended by high-quality evidence. 2. For programmatic and operational reasons, particularly in regions with generalized HIV epidemics, all pregnant and breastfeeding women with HIV should begin lifelong ART, even if they do not meet the eligibility criteria for treatment based on their own health status. This recommendation is conditional and supported by low-quality evidence. 3. In some countries, for women who are not eligible for ART based on their own health, it may be considered acceptable to discontinue the ARV regimen after the risk of mother-to-child transmission has ceased. This is a conditional recommendation based on low-quality evidence. 4. The World Health Organization (WHO) has recommended a universal treatment approach for pregnant and breastfeeding women with HIV, known as Option B+. This approach involves initiating lifelong ART for all women regardless of their CD4 count or clinical stage. Malawi was the first country to adopt this strategy, and many other high-burden countries have since followed suit. 5. While most countries have adopted Option B+, there are still important considerations regarding the risks and benefits of lifelong therapy for all women. In countries with high HIV prevalence and fertility rates, Option B+ offers public health benefits by preventing both vertical (mother-to-child) and horizontal (sexual) transmission. However, the individual benefits of lifelong ART remain unclear, leading some countries to continue advocating for Option B, which involves ART only during the transmission risk period. 6. Pregnant adolescents living with HIV face unique challenges in preventing mother-to-child transmission (PMTCT). Adolescents are at higher risk of being lost to follow-up, which can compromise the effectiveness of PMTCT strategies. This highlights the need for tailored approaches to address the specific needs of this population. 7. Evidence from studies comparing Option B and Option B+ is limited. While Option B+ simplifies service delivery and reduces the need for repeated eligibility assessments, there is no definitive evidence that it is superior to Option B in terms of clinical outcomes. However, continuous ART has been associated with slower disease progression and improved maternal health outcomes compared to interrupted treatment. 8. Discontinuing ART postpartum is associated with a decline in CD4 cell counts, particularly in women with lower baseline CD4 levels. This suggests that lifelong ART should be considered for pregnant women where feasible, as it may prevent disease progression and improve long-term health outcomes. 9. Drug resistance does not appear to be a significant issue in postpartum women who discontinue ART, provided they adhered to their ARV regimen during pregnancy. However, good follow-up and monitoring are essential to ensure optimal outcomes. 10. Lifelong ART offers several benefits, including preventing HIV transmission in future pregnancies, reducing the risk of transmission to uninfected partners, and avoiding the potential downsides of stopping and restarting ART. It also simplifies service delivery by eliminating the need for CD4 testing before initiating treatment and reduces the risk of maternal tuberculosis and disease progression. 11. The cost of implementing Option B+ is higher than Option B, but it is considered cost-effective due to the long-term savings from preventing HIV infections in children and improving maternal survival. Studies have shown that Option B+ is cost-saving or very cost-effective compared to other PMTCT strategies, particularly in high-burden settings. 12. Option B+ has been found to improve health equity by ensuring that all pregnant women with HIV receive ART as a priority, minimizing the risk of HIV transmission to children. However, the impact of Option B+ on ART access for other populations remains unclear. 13. Lifelong ART is generally acceptable to pregnant and breastfeeding women and healthcare workers. Women perceive benefits such as improved health, the ability to have more children, and protection for their partners. However, challenges include the need for better support systems for lifelong treatment and improved integration of maternal and child health services with ART programs. 14. Implementing Option B+ is feasible, but it requires strengthened data systems to track medication adherence and patient follow-up across multiple service delivery sites. Integration or co-location of maternal, newborn, and child health services with ART services may improve retention and adherence to treatment.
